{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |name=Grünfeld Defence }} == 3...d5 · Grünfeld Defence == This is the classic, and most common, starting position of the Grünfeld Defence, although d5 can be delayed if White has delayed e4 which typically happens if Nf3 is played at some stage. Most notably, the famous '''Game of the Century''' by Bobby Fischer originated from the Grünfeld Defence. The Grünfeld Defence often becomes incredibly sharp and tactical due to Black quickly striking at White's vulnerable center. Unlike the King's Indian Defence, where Black immediately fianchettoes the king bishop, here Black immediately plays 3...d5 to stop e4 (at least temporarily) and challenge White's occupation of the center. White has a range of choices, the main one is to exchange the pawns on d5 and follow up with e4 in order to displace Black's pieces. During the 1920s, European chess was in revolution, with the entry of the '''Nimzo-Indian Defence''' into mainstream opening theory. The masters of the day termed this the "Modern style". Then, in 1922, a well-known master named [[w:Ernst Grünfeld|'''Ernst Grünfeld''']] came up with a new system that started bashing the great masters of the day, including Kostic, Sämisch, Colle, and Alekhine (who famously threw his king across the room in frustration after losing to it). This came to be known as the new "hypermodern" style, and Grünfeld, true to hypermodern tastes, showed in pure form how the previously accepted classical dogma could be wrong, and that a pawn center could be an object of attack as well as a boon. The main battleground of philosophies is the '''Exchange Variation''', 4. cxd5 Nxd5 5. e4 Nxc3 6. bxc3. White's pawn center gains space, but Black has excellent play along the long, dark diagonal from a1 to h8, and can eventually target d4 with moves like ...Bg7, ...Rd8, ...c5, ...Nc6, and occasionally ...Qa5. Eventually he may also bring a bishop to fianchetto on the other diagonal, targeting e4. The more classical moves are '''[[/4. Nf3/]]''', '''[[/4. Bf4/]]''', and '''[[/4. Qb3/]]''', which are more conservative ways to fight Black's system. The pawn center still remains, but Black's counterplay is still adequate. The most positional move is '''[[/4. Bg5/]]'''. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}} '''1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5'''

{{Chess Opening Theory/Position|= |Nimzo-Indian Defence| |rd|nd|bd|qd|kd| | |rd|= |pd|pd|pd|pd| |pd|pd|pd|= | | | | |pd|nd| | |= | | | | | | | | |= | |bd|pl|pl| | | | |= | | |nl| |pl| | | |= |pl|pl| | | |pl|pl|pl|= |rl| |bl|ql|kl|bl|nl|rl|= || }} = Nimzo-Indian Defence, Rubinstein Variation = ===4. e3=== White assesses that an immediate 4...Bxc3 is not a threat, but also that 4. a3, provoking the capture, is not necessary (yet). Instead, 4. e3 simply clears the way for White's light-squared bishop to develop, usually to d3, where it helps control the all-important e4 square. Black has three main responses: * [[/4...O-O|4...O-O]] is the most common. Since Black will never castle queenside in a Nimzo-Indian, castling kingside now is a useful but still highly flexible move. * [[/4...c5|4...c5]] puts pressure on White's center immediately. Taking on c5 and accepting tripled isolated pawns (after ...Bxc3 bxc3) is right out of the question, and pushing d5 now simply creates a target, so White instead continues his development and leaves the tension. * [[/4...b6|4...b6]] is the St. Petersburg Variation (not to be confused with the [[Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...Bb4/4. Bg5|Leningrad Variation]]). This move prepares to strengthen Black's control of e4 yet further by fianchettoing a bishop to b7, though ...Ba6 is not yet out of the question. ==Sicilian Defense, Najdorf Variation, Fischer-Sozin Attack==
'''6. Bc4'''

White develops her light-squared bishop to c4, entering the Fischer-Sozin attack. Pioneered by Fischer who extensively developed the theory of it, taking inspiration from Sozin's 6. Bc4 againt the Classical Sicilian, this move was at one point White's main weapon of choice against the Najdorf. However, it then fell out of favor as ways for Black to effectively equalise against it have been found, while the English Attack's true potential to pose problems for black was discovered. Recently, it has made a resurgence with modern lines that have strong practical value.

While the bishop may be a target on c4, it eyes the f7 square against Black's king. Naturally, Black almost always responds with ...e7-e6, closing the bishop's diagonal towards the f7 square. Then, White has a few ways to develop, though she usually plays the improving move Bb3, moving the bishop to a safer square and in anticipation of ...b7-b5:

-The classical way to play this variation is to castle kingside, then launch the f-pawn forward to pressure Black's light squares and start a same-side kingside attack. While this line might be playable, it has been shown that black could equalise without facing major problems from white. The modern improvement to this variant is to first play Qf3-Qg3, making the queen an active contributor in the attack.

-Modern systems planning to castle queenside are promising. White intends to attack Black's kingside even more aggressively, and she has options of dropping explosive piece sacrifices on e6. An example line: 6...e6 7. Bb3 b5 8. Be3!? Be7 9. Qf3 Qc7 10. g4 b4 11. Nce2, where Black must play very accurately to survive.

-An important alternative is the Velimirović attack, developed by Serbian grandmaster Dragoljub Velimirović, where White plays Bb3, Be3, Qe2, O-O-O and prepares a kingside attack with Rg1 and g2-g4. This is another system where Black must be precise to survive.

-7. a4 is a reputable sideline, stopping ...b7-b5 and aiming to develop with Be3 and Qe2 just like in the Velimirović attack, but usually castles kingside and pushes f2-f4.

{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |English attack |parent=[[../|Najdorf Sicilian]] }} == 6. Be3 · English attack == 6. Be3 is the '''English attack'''. White has an idea to castle long and storm Black's kingside with their pawns. [[/6...e5|'''6...e5''']] is the '''main line'''. This drives off White's knight to b3, but weakens d5 which White will try to use as an outpost. [[/6...Ng4|'''6...Ng4''']] is the '''Anti-English'''. Black tries to avert White's plans of a kingside attack by trading off White's important dark square bishop. Whereas in the Yugoslav attack against the Dragon Sicilian, [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...Nf6/5. Nc3/5...g6/6. Be3/6...Ng4|6. Be3 Ng4?? is a mistake]] on account of 7. Bb5+! Nc6 8. Nxc6 bxc6 9. Bxc6+ Bd7 10. Bxa8, the difference in the Najdorf is that Black has played ...a6, so White does not have the resource Bb5+, therefore ...Ng4 is safe. [[/6...e6|'''6...e6''']] builds a "small centre" and transposes into a '''Scheveningen Scillian'''. This is move order ju-jitsu to play the Scheveningen without facing the Keres attack, 5...e6 6. g4!. In that line, Black cannot play 6...e5 on account of the Bb5+ resource. However, in the move order 5...a6 6. Be3 e6, Black's a6 pawn prevents Bb5+, so 7. g4!? can be met with ...e5!, a discovered attack on g4 and threatening ...exd4 with a fork. === History === 6. Be3 is the most popular way for White to combat the Najdorf. It has been played since the 1950s[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1994034 Cardoso v Jezek, 1956. Chessgames.com], but 6. Bg5 was more typical until the 1980s, when 6. Be3 was popularised by English grandmasters like [[wikipedia:Tony Miles|Tony Miles]], [[wikipedia:John Nunn|John Nunn]] and [[wikipedia:Nigel Short|Nigel Short]].e.g. [https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1114091 Short v Portish, 1985 (Candidates). Chessgames.com] The approach--long castle and pawn storm--had been the standard approach against the Dragon Sicilian, [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...Nf6/5. Nc3/5...g6/6. Be3/6...Bg7/7. f3|the Yugoslav attack]], since at least the 1930s.e.g. [https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1090706 Levenfish vs Kan, 1939. Chessgames.com] ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}} 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6.Be3

{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |King's Indian defence |eco=[[Chess/ECOE|E70]] |parent=[[../|King's Indian defence]] }} == 4...d6 == The move d6 ensures that White can't kick the Black Knight with e5. It also prepares to play e5 or c5 at some point. White has a variety of sharp choices: [[/5. Nf3|'''5. Nf3''']], the '''classical''' or '''orthodox variation''', results in a race on opposite sides: White tries to break through on the queenside before Black's forces get to the White king. Having taken the lion's share of the centre, White must now develop their minor pieces and castle. After 5...O-O 6. Be2, Black tries for the 6...e5 pawn break, and how White responds leads to the next major branching point of the theory. 5. Nf3 is by far the most popular line. [[/5. Be2|'''5. Be2''']] is commonly an alternative move order that reaches the main line position after 5...O-O 6. Nf3. However it may also be played with the idea of 6. Bg5, the Averbakh variation, while [[/5. Bg5|'''5. Bg5''']] immediately is the '''accelerated Averbakh variation'''. [[/5. f3|'''5. f3''']], the aggressive '''Sämisch variation''', is the chief sideline. White will normally castle queenside (although castling kingside can also occur) and attack along the h-file. After 5...O-O 6. Be3, Black chooses between the 6...e5 pawn break, as in the classical variation, or 6...c5, the tactical Sämisch gambit. [[/5. f4|'''5. f4''']], the '''four pawns attack''', is the most megalomaniacal variation. White gains even more space with a fourth pawn in on the fourth rank. Black must react quickly to avoid getting crushed by White's centre, but in the long term they can exploit the weak squares the advancing pawns has left behind. This is the most popular sideline at the amateur level. [[/5. h3|'''5. h3''']] is the quirky '''Makogonov variation''', which stops a knight or bishop from getting into g4 while retaining the option of Nf3. [[/5. g3|'''5. g3''']], the '''deferred fianchetto''', is the most positional variation. Normally the position is fluid. Black usually exchanges his e-pawn for White's d-pawn, Black tries to play on the queenside dark squares and against e4, while White lines his forces up against d6 and the kingside. [[/5. Nge2|'''5. Nge2''']] is the '''Kramer variation'''. 5. Nge2 intends Ng3, keeping the option of f3, similar to the Sämisch. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}} '''1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 g6 3. {{Chess Opening Theory/Position |English attack |parent=[[../|English attack]] }} == 6...e5 == 6...e5 is the most popular and most unbalancing response to the English attack. The pawn drives off the White's well-placed knight from d4 to a more passive square. Although this creates an outpost on d5, Black is saying, basically, that it is irrelevant to the play on the wings, while White is saying that Black will be lost if d5 is occupied. White must save their knight, usually to [[/7. Nb3|'''7. Nb3''']], and Black's main move is 7...Be6, increasing their control of d5. White's plans include playing f3, Qd2, long castling, and storm on the kingside with pawns. Less popular is [[/7. Nf3|'''7. Nf3''']], where the threat of Ng5 discourages 7...Be6. The knight prevents f3 and puts the pawn-storm idea on the back-burner. White concentrates on fighting for control of the d5 square instead. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}}. 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6.Be3 e5

{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |King's Indian defence |eco=[[Chess/ECOE|E70]] |parent=[[../|King's Indian defence]] }} == 5. Nf3 == White develops their knight and seems to have an iron grip on the centre. All their pawns are defended and they have no weaknesses. [[/5...O-O|'''5...O-O''']] is the main move. After getting their king to safety, Black is finally ready to strike back at the centre. Castling is an important preparatory move. If '''5...e5?''' immediately, Black gets the worse of it after 6. dxe5 dxe5 7. Qxd8+ Kxd8 8. Nxe5 Nxe4 9. Nxe4 Bxe5 10. White creates a massive pawn centre and has full control over the middle of the board ... for now. This is a dangerous line for Black, and if they don't play correctly, they will be knocked off the board by White's advancing army. However, if Black can survive the initial onslaught, they will have the better game since White will have many weak squares in their camp that their pawns can't defend. For this reason, the Four Pawns Attack isn't seen frequently at the highest levels of chess, although it's still very viable at the amateur level. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}}. == 5.e4 ==
This move greedily grabs central space. Since Nf6 or Nb6 would leave black without enough pressure in the center, Nb4 misplaces the knight only to create the obvious threat of Qxd4 followed by Nc2, Nxc3 is forced. Although d4 is strengthened, the queenside weakens, and the a1-h8 diagonal loosens up.  That is why g6 and Bg7 is played in the Gruenfeld Defence. Black will now play to dismantle white's central ambitions. Usually, Black advances the c-pawn, and then he uses his e-pawn to dismantle white's center. Also, Nb4?? loses to Qa4+ Nc6 d5.

After e4, White has a dangerous center. Black must pressure it or risk a cramped, passive game. The only good move is Nxc3, else play resembles the dubious Marshall defence.

* [[/3...d6|3...d6 · Classical Variation]] * [[/3...Nxe4|3...Nxe4 · Damiano variation]] * [[/3...Nc6|3...Nc6 · Stafford gambit]]|eco=[[Chess/ECOC|C42]] }} == 3. Nxe5 == White picks up the undefended pawn. This is the classical continuation of Petrov's defence aka the Russian game. Before Black can recover the pawn, they must drive White's knight away, or else choose to gambit it. === Recover the pawn === The natural move [[/3...Nxe4|'''3...Nxe4!?''']], the '''Damiano variation''', doesn't actually recover the pawn, as after 4. Qe2 Black runs into difficulties with pins on the open e-file. The classic beginner's trap is 4...Nf6?? 5. Nc6+, winning Black's queen. (Instead, Black can sacrifice the pawn in this line. See below.) Therefore, in order to recover the pawn, Black has to drive White's knight away first. [[/3...d6|'''3...d6''']] 4. Nf3 Nxe4 is the '''main line'''. Without White's knight on the e-file, should White play 5. Qe2 Black may defuse it with 5...Qe7, defending and unpinning the knight. === Gambit the pawn === [[/3...Nc6|'''3...Nc6?!''']] is the most "in vogue" at amateur levels: the explosive '''Stafford gambit'''. After 4. Nxc6 dxc6, Black has sacrificed their pawn but opened the position, ready to play ...Bc5 and ...Ng4 for a swift attack on White's f2 square. Black may also give up the pawn with [[/3...Nxe4|'''3...Nxe4!?''']] 4. Qe2 Qe7, the Kholmov gambit. After 5. Qxe4 d6 6. d4 dxe5 7. dxe5 (trading knights) Nc6, it's often too perilous for White to hold onto the extra pawn. [[/3...d5|'''3...d5?''']] is a gambit favoured by [[w:Baadur Jobava|Baadur Jobava]]. == Theory table == {{ChessTable}} '''1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nf6 3. Nxe5'''

{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Modern attack |eco=[[Chess/ECOC|C43]] |parent=[[../|Russian game]] }} == 3. d4 · Modern attack or Steinitz attack == The chief sideline to 3. Nxe5, with 3. d4 White seeks to open the centre immediately and offers Black their choice of pawns to capture. [[/3...exd4|'''3...exd4!?''']] is playable but less conventional as it allows 4. e5! to kick the knight. Typically this leads to trading both d- and e-pawns and opening the centre fully: the main continuation is 4...Ne4 5. Qxd4 (the '''Centre attack''') d5 (defends knight) 6. exd6 e.p. Nxd6 7. Nc3, although there are some sidelines (5. Qe2 was advocated by '''Steinitz'''; 5. Bb4+ is the '''Tal gambit'''). [[/3...Nxe4|'''3...Nxe4''']] is the main line and leads to a trade of e-pawns. White could retake immediately (4. Nxe5 or 4. exd4) but the normal move order is 4. Bd3 d5 5. Nxe5, where after ...d5 first Black doesn't have ...d6 to shoo the knight away. [[/3...d5|'''3...d5''']], the '''Symmetrical variation''', passes the decision on what to take first back to White. Since Black has played ...d5 of their own volition, White may choose 4. Nxe5 and the positions can transpose after 4...Nxe4 5. Bd3 (4...dxe4? 5. Bc4 [threatening Nxf7] Be6 6. Bxe6 fxe6 and Black has isolated double e-pawns{{chess/not|++}}). [[/3...d6|'''3...d6''']] transposes to the [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nf6|Nimzowitsch variation of the Philidor defence]]. === History === Jaenisch credited Petrov with 3. d4,{{Cite book |title=Jaenisch's chess preceptor: a new analysis of the openings of games |last=de Jaenisch |first=C. F. |publisher=Longman & co. |year=1847 |location=London |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=hvd.hn52dv&seq=5 |translator-last=Walker |translator-first=George}} (translation of {{Cite book |title=Analyse nouvelle des ouvertures du jeu des échecs |last=de Jaenisch |first=C. F. |publisher=Gartner |year=1842 |pages=126-147}}) who had perhaps the earliest games with it.[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1257912 Petrov v Allies, 1837 - Chessgames.com]; [https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1257913 Petrov v. Jaenisch, 1844 - Chessgames.com] A later advocate of the line was [[wikipedia:Wilhelm Steinitz|Steinitz]], who wrote in his 1889 book:{{Cite book |title=Modern Chess Instructor |last=Steintiz |first=Wilhelm |publisher=G. P. Putnam's Sons |year=1889 |location=London |pages=116-139}}
As regards its [2...Nf6] merits as a defence various authorities have expressed different opinions on the subject, but all agreed hitherto that 3 Kt×P [3. Nxe5] was White's best continuation though it was generally admitted that this line of attack only retained the advantage of the first move by proper play on the other side. We think however that the superior position at least can be proved for the first player by the attack 3 P—Q4 [3. d4] which has hitherto been almost ignored.
Because of his endorsement, some opening books (e.g. Chess.com's opening explorer) give 3. d4 the appellation ''Steinitz attack'' instead. Others (e.g. Lichess.org's) reserve it for the continuation 3...exd4 4. e5 Ne4 5. Qe2, which Steinitz preferred to 5. Qxd4. 3. d4 particularly came into vogue in the 1990s, where it was adopted at the highest levels including by Kasparov[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chess.pl?pid=15940&side=white&eco=C43 Garry Kasparov games in the Petrov, Modern Attack - Chessgames.com] including [https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1067286 Kasparov v. Karpov, 1990 - Chessgames.com] and Ivanchuk.[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chess.pl?pid=12183&side=white&eco=C43 Vasyl Ivanchuck games in the Petrov, Modern Attack - Chessgames.com] =Theory table= {{ChessTable}} '''1. e4 e5 2. pages.wikitext:
{{Chess Opening Theory/Position
|Philidor defence
|parent=[[../|Philidor defence]]
}}
== 3. d4 ==

White attacks e5 again and threatens to win the pawn. Black must deal with the threat: trade, defend, or counterattack?

=== Trade the pawn ===

If Black allows White to trade into them, dxe5, Black won't even be able to recapture using their d-pawn because it is pinned to their queen, so doing so would allow an unfavourable queen trade. 

Most straightforwardly then, Black should trade first. [[/3...exd4|'''3...exd4''']] is the exchange Philidor. This is the main line.

=== Defend the pawn ===

Black can try defending the pawn. The chief way to do so is [[/3...Nd7|'''3...Nd7''']], the Hanham variation. White usually replies 4. Bc4, targeting  the vulnerable f7 pawn and threatening a mating trap if Black continues to develop normally. No other defence is sound:

* [[/3...Bg4|'''3...Bg4''']] is a popular amateur reply, but doesn't succeed in defending the pawn. Though Black thinks to pin the knight to White's queen, after 4. dxe5 dxe5 5. Qxd8+ (trades queens and unpins the knight) Kxd8, White's knight is unpinned and can take back on e5 anyway. If 4... Bxf3 first, as in the [[wikipedia:Opera Game|Opera Game]], 5. Qxf3 dxe5 6. Bc4 and White is threatening a crushing attack on f7. But, 3...Bg4?! can be used to gambit the pawn (see below)
* [[/3...Nc6|'''3...Nc6?!''']] (transposing into a sort of 'declined' [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4|Scotch game]]) is unpalatable for Black. While this looks like a more natural square for the knight than d7, it can be met with either 4. e5, kicking the knight, or 4. Bb5, pinning it (as a consequence of Black having played d6 first) and transposing into a Old Steinitz Spanish, which is not a defence held in very high regard. 
* [[/3...f6|'''3...f6?''']] defends e5 with the f pawn, but gives White more time to extend their development lead and exploit the weakened kingside.

=== Counterattack ===

Or, Black can leave the pawn undefended and counterattack White's e-pawn instead. There are two approaches: 

* [[/3...Nf6|'''3...Nf6''']], the Nimzowitsch variation, plans to meet 4. dxe5 with 4...Nxe4, after which the natural looking 5. exd6? Bxd6 leads to equality for Black.
* [[/3...f5|'''3...f5?!''']] was Philidor's Romantic recommendation, with the understanding that trading a more peripheral f-pawn to eliminate the more valuable central e-pawn is surely advantageous. 
:White has their choice of captures 4. dxe5?! fxe4 (kicks knight) 5. Ng5 d5 and while the engine still favours White, the position is unusual and perilous. 4. exf5 and the pawn can be recovered by 4...Bxf5, or the knight kicked first with 4...e4. 
:However, 3...f5?! is simply too weakening. 4. Bc4 and Black is soon facing a choice of allowing a fork by Nf7 or Qh4+ and the annihilation of their kingside.

=== Gambit the pawn ===

* While [[/3...Bg4|'''3...Bg4''']] doesn't defend the e5 pawn (see above), it allows Black to gambit it and play 4...Nd7, the Albin-Blackburne gambit. Black gives up their two central pawns for one of White's central pawns and sped up development.

{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Scotch game |eco=[[Chess/ECOC|C44]] |parent=[[../|Scotch game]] |responses= }} == 3...exd4 == Black takes the pawn in the centre. [[/4. Nxd4|'''4. Nxd4''']], recapturing the pawn, is the main line. White centralises their knight, supported by their queen. Black has a chance to take the initiative and develop with tempo, attacking White's centre with 4...Bc5 or 4...Nf6. Alternatively, White can gambit the pawn and not recapture it: [[/4. Bc4|'''4. Bc4''']] is the '''Scotch Gambit'''. White leaves the pawn in peace and tries to establish attacking pressure with a lead in development. [[/4. c3|'''4. c3''']] is the '''Göring Gambit'''. Similar to the [[Chess/Danish Gambit|Danish gambit]], White offers one or two further pawns to get a lead in development. [[/4. Ng5|'''4. Ng5?''']] is a trap line, the idea being to sacrifice the knight on f7 to lure out Black's king. It is dubious and can be disarmed by best play, but scores well in amateur databases. 4...h6 5. Nxf7 Kxf7 6. Bc4+ and Black must avoid 6...Ke8??, else 7. Qh5+ leads to forced mate. ==Theory table== {{ChessTable}} '''1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4'''

It puts pressure on the e pawn, and aims to protect the d5 square. This variation is marginally preferred to the 2...d5 response, and is statistically a better win-rate for Black (as per ChessBase.com). ==White’s Responses== 3.[[/3. e5|e5]] immediately pressures the Black knight, and is by far the most popular response. It also continues White’s assault on the centre, and aims to reinforce with d4. 3.[[/3. d3|d3]] and 3.[[/3. d4|d4]] are playable, but more passive. d3 aims to protect the e pawn, while d4 simply continues with White’s original plan of controlling the d4 square - the goal of the Alapin opening. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}}. :'''1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6''' {| border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="4" |- ! ! align="left" | 3 |- ! align="right" | Sicilian, Alapin | [[/3. e5|e5]]

pages.wikitext:
{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Alapin Sicilian |eco=[[Chess/ECOB|B22]] |parent=[[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5|Sicilian defence]] → [[../|Alapin variation]] }} == 2...d5 == Black is threatening to take on e4. White's best option is to take first, with [[/3. exd5|'''3. exd5''']]. After [[/3. exd5|'''3. exd5''']] the main line continues 3...Qxd5, the Barmen variation, and White doesn't have Nc3 to kick the queen away. After 4. d4, it is possible for Black to win a pawn and go into an endgame,4...cxd4 5. cxd4 Nc6 6. Nf3 Bg4 7. Nc3 Bxf3 8. gxf3 Qxd4 9. Qxd4 Nxd4 10. Nb5!{{chess/not|+}} however White has adequate compensation and better practical chances. A more common plan is to leave White with an isolated queen's pawn position and control d5 with ...e6 and ...Nf6.e.g. 4...Nc6 5. Nf3 Bg4 6. Be2 cxd4 7. cxd4 e6 8. Nc3 Qa5 9. h3 Bh5 10. O-O Nf6{{chess/not|+}}. Black's other line is 3...Nf6, christened the anti-Alapin gambit, which is similar to the [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. f4/2...d5|Tal gambit]]. White has the time to defend the d-pawn, but Black is eager to give some material for rapid development, e.g. 4. c4 e6 5. dxe6 Bxe6. === Bad moves === A quick round up of the White's other turn three options, which they should discard: White cannot play Nc3 to defend the pawn, as their c-pawn already occupies c3. '''3. e5!?''' allows Black to play ...Bf5 & ...e6, reaching an advance French-style position with the strict improvement that Black has been able to develop their queen's bishop outside of the pawn chain first. Black has equalised. '''3. d3?!''' to defend e4 leaves the pawn on c3 out of place. If White avoids taking on d5, they allow Black easy development and plenty of space, e.g. 3...Nc6 4. Nd2 Nf6 5. Ngf3 e5 6. Be2 Be7 7. O-O O-O{{chess/not|-}}. Black could also consider playing d4 themselves: 3...d4 4. cxd4 cxd4 5. Qa4+ Nc6 6. Nf3{{chess/not|-}}. '''3. d4?''' and Black is better after 3...dxe4 4. dxc5 Qxd1+ 5. Kxd1 Nf6{{chess/not|-}}. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}} :'''1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5'''

pages.wikitext:
{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |name=Valencian variation |eco=[[Chess/ECOB|B01]] |parent=[[../|Scandinavian defence]] }} == 3...Qd8 · Valencian variation == Black un-develops their queen. Back on d8 she is very safe but has limited scope, and Black will have to spend some more time developing her again later. White now has a free hand to continue development. The main move is [[/4. d4|'''4. d4''']], taking space in the centre and allowing the queen's bishop into the game. The main line continues 4...Nf6 5. Nf3 Bg4 6. h3 Bxf3 7. Qxf3 c6 (7...Qxd4?? allows 8. Qxb7 winning Black's rook). === History === 3...Qd8 is the continuation depicted in ''[[w:Scachs d'amor|Scachs d'amor]]'', the 15th century Valencian poem depicting a chess game between [[w:Francesc de Castellví|Francesc de Castellví]] (as Mars) and [[w:Narcís Vinyoles|Narcís Vinyoles]] (as Venus). It is notable as perhaps the oldest recorded chess game.[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1259987 Castellvi v. Vinyoles, 1475. Chessgames.com][https://scachsdamor.org/ English translation of ''Sachs d'amor'' - sachsdamor.org] Prior to the 20th century, 3...Qd8 was often considered the main line. [[w:Carl Jaenisch|Carl Jaenisch]] and [[w:Howard Staunton|Howard Staunton]] both characterised it as "best" and gave the continuation 4. d4 Bf5 5. Nf3 e6 6. Bc4, White stands better.{{Cite book |title=Jaenisch's chess preceptor: a new analysis of the openings of games |last=de Jaenisch |first=C. F. |publisher=Longman & co. |year=1847 |location=London |url=https://archive.org/details/jaenischs-chess-preceptor |translator-last=Walker |translator-first=George |page=40}} (translation of {{Cite book |title=Analyse nouvelle des ouvertures du jeu des échecs |last=de Jaenisch |first=C. F. |publisher=Gartner |year=1842}}){{Cite book |title=The Chess Player's Handbook |last=Staunton |first=Howard |publisher=Henry G. Bohn |year=1847 |location=London |pages=377 |url=https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_fd8CAAAAYAAJ}} In the 1960s, 3...Qd8 experienced a revival after it was played by [[w:David Bronstein|David Bronstein]] against [[w:Andrija Fuderer|Andrija Fuderer]] in 1959.[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1034081 Bronstein v Fuderer, 1959. Chessgames.com] Bronstein's game featured the older line 4. d4 Nf6, while other grandmasters, including [[w:Karl Robatsch|Karl Robatsch]], explored fianchetto systems with 4.d4 g6 and a later ...Ng8–h6.[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1044011 Fischer v Robatsch, 1962. Chessgames.com] The 3...Qd8 variation as a whole remains playable, although it is now considered somewhat passive. It is played particularly by IMs [[w:John Bartholomew (American chess player)|John Bartholomew]] and Daniel Lowinger, and by the GMs David Garcia Ilundain and Nikola Djukic. == Sample game == '''Robert Fischer versus Karl Robatsch, 1962.'''
Varna Olympiad, Varna, Bulgaria. '''1. e4 d5 2. exd5 Qxd5 3. Nc3 Qd8''' The Valencian variation, an ancient approach to the Scandinavian. '''4. d4 g6''' Black reinvigorates the opening with hypermodern ideas, giving up the centre with plans to attack it. ...g6 prepares to fianchetto the bishop. They delay ...Nf6, intending ...Nh6 and ...Nf5. '''5. Bf4 Bg7 6. Qd2!''' White's pawn on d4 is not really hanging. If 6...Bxd4?? 7. O-O-O pins the bishop, and 7...c5 8. Nb5 (threatens Nc7+) Na6 9. c3 {{chess/not|+++}} or 7...Nc6 8. Bb5 Bd7 9. Nd5 e5 10. Nf3 {{chess/not|+++}} and "Black will never get out of the opening alive."{{Cite book |title=My 60 Memorable Games |last=Fischer |first=Bobby |publisher=Simon & Schuster |year=1969 |location=New York |url=https://archive.org/details/my60memorablegam00fisc |chapter=41 - A bright cameo}} After 6...Qd2 Qxd4 7. Qxd4 Bxd4, Fischer gives 8. Nb5 Bb6 9. Nxc7+ Bxc7 10. Bxc7; an improvement is 8. Nd5! Bb6 9. Bxc7!, and the line continues 8...Be6 10. Bb5+ Nc6 11. Nxb6 axb6 12. Bxb6 {{chess/not|++}}. 6. Qd2 makes it impossible for Black to achieve ...Nh6. '''6...Nf6 7. O-O-O c6 8. Bh6 O-O?!''' Better would be for Black to concede they won't be castling kingside and play 8...Bxh6 9. Qxh6. Castling short, into White's attack, leaves Black beyond hope. '''9. h4 Qa5 10. h5''' White wishes to tear open Black's king's side and expose the king, e.g. 10...Rd8? 11. hxg6 fxg6 12. Bxg7 Kxg7 13. Qh6+. '''6...gxh5''' Best was 6...Bf5 so that after 7. hxg6 the bishop could retake. '''11. Bd3 Nbd7 12. Nge2 Rd8 13. g4''' White can offer another pawn for sacrifice because of the vulnerability of Black's king and strength of White's attack. If 13...Nxg4?! 14. Rdg1! wins with 14...Ndf6 15. Bxg7 Kxg7 16. f3. '''13...Nf8 14. gxh5 Ne6 15. Rdg1''' White now attacks along the open g-file. '''15...Kh8 16. Bxg7+ Nxg7 17. Qh6 Rg8 18. Rg5 Qd8 19. Rhg1 Nf5?''' A blunder of a piece. '''20. Bxf5 1-0''' White resigns. If 20...Bxf5 21. Rxg8+ Qxg8 22. Rxg8+ Rxg8 {{chess/not|+++}}. This game killed the reputation of the 4...g6 line. Emms writes it "has been under a cloud ever since the crushing win for White in Fischer-Robatsch, Varna Olympiad 1962."{{Cite book |title=The Scandinavian |last=Emms |first=John |publisher=Everyman Chess |year=2004 |edition=2nd |location=London |pages=97-100}} ==Theory table== {{ChessTable}} {{Chess/theory table |line1=4. d4 Nf6 5. Nf3 Bg4 6. h3 Bxf3 7. Qxf3 c6 |name1=Valencian variation |eval1={{chess/not|+}} |line2=4. ... ... 5. ... c6 6. Bc4 Bf5 7. Ne5 e6 |name2=Ilundain variation |eval2={{chess/not|+}} |line3=4. ... g6 5. Bf4 Bg7 6. Qd2! Nf6 |eval3={{chess/not|+}} }} {{ChessMid}} ==References== {{reflist}} === See also === {{Wikipedia|Scandinavian Defence}} *{{Cite book |title=The 3...Qd8 Scandinavian: Simple and Strong |last=Lowinger |first=Daniel |publisher=Russell Enterprises |year=2013 |isbn=978-1936490769}} *[https://www.chessable.com/im-john-bartholomews-scandinavian-defense/course/79/ ''IM John Batholomew's Scandinavian Defense''], Chessable.com. {{Chess Opening Theory/Footer}}

{{Chess Opening Theory/Position|= |Queen's Gambit Accepted| |rd|nd|bd|qd|kd|bd|nd|rd|= |pd|pd|pd| |pd|pd|pd|pd|= | | | | | | | | |= | | | | | | | | |= | | |pd|pl| | | | |= | | | | |pl| | | |= |pl|pl| | | |pl|pl|pl|= |rl|nl|bl|ql|kl|bl|nl|rl|= || }} =Queen's Gambit Accepted= ===3. e3=== This move is not quite so popular as the main lines 3. e4 or 3. Nf3, but respectable nonetheless. It is a more conservative move. White opts to defend d4 instead of taking the center with pawns. Black cannot try to hold on to his c-pawn because of the famous trap 3...b5? (black should pursue development with ...e5) 4. a4! (getting the base of the pawn chain) c6? (further weakening the h1 to a8 diagonal) 5. axb5! cxb5?? (it would still be better to develop now, even though white will end with a pawn up or a huge lead in development) 6. Qf3! when Black must part with at least a minor piece because the weak h1 to a8 diagonal can't be defended anymore. Note: 6... Bb7 loses to 7. Qxb7. Common Black continuations include: *3... e5 - a newer, aggressive move that tries to open up the position and likely results in an isolated queen pawn for white (4. dxe5? fails to 4...Qxd1! when white loses castling rights). *3... e6 - The more classical, conservative approach, although it results in limited mobility for the light-squared bishop. *3... Nf6 - Typical developing move. White then usually takes the c-pawn. ==Theory table== {{ChessTable}} '''1. d4 d5 2. c4 dxc4 3. e3'''

Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. e5/3...Bf5

{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |name=Advance variation |eco=[[Chess/ECOB|B12]] |parent=[[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6|Caro-Kann]] → [[../|Advance variation]] }} == 3...Bf5 == This is the main continuation to the advance variation. Black develops their bishop so that they may continue ...e6 to unleash their other bishop without restricting this one. The development of the bishop outside of the pawn chain is the key positional advantage difference between the Caro-Kann and the French. White's choice here is between patient development and positional play, and attempting to capitalise on Black's bishop, which is unsupported and potentially vulnerable on f5. === Patient development === White has the space advantage, now they just wish to get their pieces developed and surely they will have a good game. The main line is [[/4. Nf3|'''4. Nf3''']], the '''Short variation''', 4...e6 5. Be2. White develops their kingside and prepares to answer ...c5 ...cxd4 with Nxd4. Once Black has played ...e6, their king's bishop supports the 5...c5 pawn break, though it is not forced and another ideae.g. [https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1977122 Kasimdzhanov v Howell, 2019. Chessgames.com] is to develop their pieces before breaking on the kingside with ...f6. Other moves include [[/4. Nd2|'''4. Nd2''']], intending Nb3 and control of c5. === Assail Black's bishop === White has several ideas to harass it. In increasing order of audaciousness: [[/4. Nc3|'''4. Nc3''']] is the sharp '''van der Wiel attack'''. White has a plan to harangue Black's bishop with g4 and h4-h5, and first includes Nc3 to take away the e4 square from the bishop. 4...e6 5. g4 Bg6 6. Nge2 c5 7. h4 (threatening 8. h5 winning the bishop) h5 8. Nf4 Bh7 9. Nxh5{{Chess/not}}; White wins a pawn but the line is sharp and offers Black good compensation. [[/4. h4|'''4. h4''']], the '''Tal variation''', is a more direct way of attacking Black's bishop. If 4...e6?? the bishop cannot be saved: 5. g4 Be4 6. f3 Bg6 7. h5{{chess/not|++}}, showing that White doesn't have to include Nc3 if they're willing to play f3. 4...h6 provides an escape square but allows 5. g4 Be4 6. f3 Bh7 7. e6! Qd6 (if 7...fxe6?, Black has no hope of getting in the liberating ...e6 pawn move) 8. exf7+ Kxf7{{chess/not|+}}. More common is 4...h5 5. Bd3 Bxd3 6. Qxd3 e6{{chess/not}}. [[/4. g4|'''4. g4!?''']], the '''Bayonet attack''', is an even more direct way of attacking Black's bishop. In this order, 4...Be4 5. f3 Bg6 6. e6 (6. h4?! h5, White isn't in time to trap the bishop) Qd6 7. exf7+ Bxf7{{Chess/not|+}}. White has severely weakened their kingside before they've castled or developed any pieces, so was it really worth it? === Other moves === [[/4. Bd3|'''4. Bd3?!''']], where White trades off Black's bad bishop for their good one, is considered inferior but a popular amateur try. '''4. f4!?''', White takes more space on the kingside before playing Nf3. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}} '''1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5'''

== 3...c5 · Botvinnik-Carls Defence ==

This is Black's second most common option, after [[../3...Bf5|3...Bf5]]. It is an attack on the base of White's pawn chain.

After [[/4. dxc5|'''4. dxc5''']], Black can eventually recover the pawn with ...e6 and ...Bxc5, though there is usually no hurry and it's not in White's best interests to hold onto the c-pawn too tightly. One line is 4...Nc6 (the e5-pawn is now loose) 5. f4 e6 6. Be3 d4 7. Bf2 Bxc5{{chess/not|+}}. 

[[/4. Nf3|'''4. Nf3''']] allows 4...cxd4 and prepares to recapture the pawn with the knight. 5. Nxd4 Nc6 (e5 is loose) 6. Nxc6 bxc6 7. Bd3 prevents Black from developing their light-square bishop actively.

[[/4. c3|'''4. c3''']], preparing to recapture on d4 with a pawn, is a minor sideline but very common in amateur play. Black does not need to take d4 straight away: they can leave the tension and focus on development. 

=== History ===
This line is named after World Champion [[w:Mikhail Botvinnik|Mikhail Botvinnik]] and [[w:Carl Carls|Carl Carls]]. 

Carls had one of the earliest appearances of the line in Breslau, 1912.<ref>[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1284285 Treybal v Carls, 1912. Chessgames.com]</ref> However the line remained uncommon until Botvinnik relied upon it in his [[w:World Chess Championship 1961|1961 rematch]] with [[w:Mikhail Tal|Mikhail Tal]].<ref>[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1032564 Tal v Botvinnik, 1961. Chessgames.com (Round 4)]</ref><ref>[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1032566 Tal v Botvinnik, 1961. Chessgames.com (Round 6)]</ref><ref>[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1032570 Tal v Botvinnik, 1961. Chessgames.com (Round 8)]</ref> Botvinnik won the match and regained the World Championship title, although he had poor results (2 draws and a loss) with this variation.

{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Russian game |parent=[[../|Russian game]] |eco=[[Chess/ECOC|C42]] }} == 3...d6 == White's knight is under attack and must be moved, then it is safe for Black to pick up the pawn. [[/4. Nf3|'''4. Nf3''']] is the overwhelmingly common choice, and Black retakes the pawn with 4...Nxe4. This reaches the main junction of the Russian game where there are several theoretical continuations; the main line is 5. d4, the classical attack. [[/4. Nd3|'''4. Nd3!?''']], the '''Karklins-Martinovsky variation''' has been tried occasionally, notably played by Magnus Carlsen in the 2018 World Chess Championship against Fabiano Caruana.{{cite web |url=https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1937789 |title=Magnus Carlsen vs. Fabiano Caruana, 2018 |website=Chessgames.com}} Temporarily blocking the d-pawn, White's knight will eventually make way for it by rerouting to f4. 4...Nxe4 5. Qe2 Qe7 6. Nf4 Nf6 7. d4 Qxe2+ 8. Bxe2 Nc6 {{chess/not|+}}. [[/4. Nc4|'''4. Nc4!?''']], the '''Paulsen attack''', avoids blocking the d-pawn, but is no more effective than 4. Nd3 according to the engine. The knight usually ends up falling back to e3. [[/4. Nxf7|'''4. Nxf7?!''']] is the '''Cochrane gambit''', a double-edged but dubious gambit. White sacrifices their knight to drive Black's king out into the open and keep the initiative. After 4...Kxf7 5. d4 Nxe4? is a mistake due to 6. Qh5+ g6 7. Qd5+ Kg7 8. Qxe4 {{chess/not|++}}. ==Theory table== {{ChessTable}} '''1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nf6 3. Nxe5 d6'''

pages.title: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...Nc6
pages.wikitext:
{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Stafford gambit |eco=[[Chess/ECOC|C42]] |parent=[[../|Russian game]] }} == 3...Nc6? · Stafford gambit == Rather than try to recover the pawn (as in [[../3...d6|3...d6]] 4. Nf3 Nxe4), Black invites White to trade knights. Black's plan after 4. Nxc6 is to take back with the d pawn, opening lines for their bishop and queen. They have entered the dubious but dangerous '''Stafford gambit'''. === Accepting the gambit === [[/4. Nxc6|'''4. Nxc6''']] should be to White's advantage: being up one pawn in material, trading knights brings them closer to consolidating their lead. The engine doesn't find this gambit sound for Black (Stockfish evaluates the game as around +1.4 after 4...dxc6), however, the line is so sharp that Black often has practical success, especially in faster time controls. Black plays for an aggressive attack on White's kingside and the f2 square. White must play carefully and solidly and attempt to win the long game. === Declining the gambit === [[/4. d4|'''4. d4''']] is the best way to '''decline''' the Stafford gambit. It allows Black to take the pawn back (most accurately with 4...Qe7 5. Nc3 Nxe5 6. dxe5 Qxe5 {{chess/not|+}}). The game can be sharp, especially in the 4...Nxe4!? line where White may set some traps for Black. 4. d4 gives away some of White's advantage but the game is still in White's favour. [[/4. Nf3|'''4. Nf3''']] declines the gambit but gives away all of White's advantage. White returns the pawn and it leads to an even game (e.g. 4...Nxe4 5. Qe2 Qe7 6. Nc3 Nxc3 7. dxc3 Qxe2+ 8. Bxe2 {{Chess/not}}). A White player who has been burnt by the Stafford before or is dead-set on playing a Petrov defence position may prefer it as a quieter continuation. After 4...Nxe4, play resembles a main line Russian game (cf. [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...d6/4. Nf3/4...Nxe4|3...d6 4. Nf3 Nxe4]]). White can chose their preferred Russian game line, including 5. d4, 5. Qe2, or 5. Nc3 for games resembling a Classical, Cozio, or Nimzowitsch variation but where Black has played Nc6 instead of d6. In Hou v Dubov 2021, White declined with 4. Nf3 and transposed into an Exchange French position down a tempo.[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=2054847 Hou v Dubov 2021 - Chessgames.com]. 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nf6 3. Nxe5 Nc6 4. Nf3 Nxe4 5. d3 Nf6 6. d4 d5 7. Bd3 was played and it is Black to move; compare [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. d4/2...d5/3. exd5/3...exd5/4. Nf3|1. e4 e6 2. d4 d5 3. exd5 exd5 4. Nf3]] Nf6 5. Bd3 Nc6 and it is White to move. [[/4. Nc3|'''4. Nc3??''']] transposes into the [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Nxe5|Halloween gambit]]. White sacrifices the knight in exchange for initiative and space. The gambit is unsound but offers some practical success against the unprepared player. === History === 3...Nc6 was tried by [[wikipedia:Howard Staunton|Howard Staunton]] in a consultation game in 1857.[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1271967 Allies v Staunton 1857 - Chessgames.com] White accepted the gambit and defended themselves admirably against Staunton's threats with a defence that looks very close to the modern refutation, including d3, Be2, and c3. There is record of a 1950 correspondence game between Irving Lowens and a "Stafford" where Black played this line. Who Stafford was, however, goes unrecorded.[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1243149 Lowens v Stafford, 1950 - Chessgames.com] Lowens resigned after 6 moves, succumbing to Black's pressure on f2 (see sample game). 3...Nc6 remained very rare until it had some revival in the 1990s. In the 2020s it was popularised by online chess streamers, especially International Master [[wikipedia:Eric Rosen (chess player)|Eric Rosen]] who used it to defeat Grandmaster [[wikipedia:Sergey Erenburg|Sergey Erenburg]] at the 2024 World Blitz Championship in 14 moves.[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=2820214 Erenburg v Rosen 2024 - Chessgames.com] Because of this, a lot of the Stafford gambit's surprise value has diminished. While still vanishingly rare in tournament games, 3...Nc6?! is now the most common move for Black in the Lichess player database as of 2025. == Sample game == '''Irving Lowens vs Stafford, 1950.'''
'''Correspondence.''' '''1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nf6 3. Nxe5 Nc6?''' Black offers the gambit. Rather than recover their pawn, they allow White to trade knights in return for a development advantage and attacking chances. '''4. Nxc6 dxc6''' Taking back with the pawn 4...bxc6?! is far less sharp than the text move, which immediately brings the bishop to influence White's king's side and opens the d-file for the queen. '''5. e5!? Ne4 6. d3??''' Since from e4 Black's knight pressures White's position, in particular the f2 square, White thinks to kick it away immediately with d3. However, Black does not have to move the knight! Better was 6. d4, preparing Bd3 to drive the knight away. The pawn controls c5, and the queen now controls d4 and prevents ideas with ...Qd4. If 6...Bc5 anyway, 7. dxc5 Qxd1 8. Kxd1 Nxf2+ 9. Ke1 Nxh1 {{Chess/not|++}} is still to White's advantage (Black is up material but their knight is probably never getting out and White can pick it up later), but better is 7. c3: Black's bishop is out of the attack and White is ready to play Bd3!. If 6...Qh4, the threat of 7...Qxf2# can be parried with 7. Be3 or 7. Qf3. {{Chess/board | moves = 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nc6 4.Nxc6 dxc6 5.e5 Ne4 6.d3 Bc5 | frame = 1 | float = right | caption = Final position. Black threatens mate in two with '''Bxf2+ Ke2 Bg4#'''. * If '''7. dxe4''' Black wins White's queen (7...Bxf2+ 8. Kxf2 Qxd1). * If '''7. Be3''' Black is up the exchange (7...Bxe3 8. fxe3 Qh4+ 9. g3 Nxg3 10. hxg3 Qxh1). }} '''6...Bc5! 0-1''' White's problem is that their d-pawn is pinned to their queen. If they take 7. dxe4 Bxf2+! 8. Ke2 (8. Kxf2 Qxd1) Bg4+ deflects White's king from defence of queen. However, if White does not take on e4, say 7. Nc3??, the threat is still 7...Bxf2+! 8. Ke2 Bg4#. White could try to move their queen e.g. 7. Qf3, which defends f2 and avoids their queen becoming forked by ...Nxf2. Then 7...Nxf2 8. Rg1 only wins Black back the pawn. However, 8...Qd4! and the pressure is simply too much. 9. Be3 Qxe3+ 10. Qxe3 Bxe3 {{Chess/not|---}} and White's position is hopeless. Most resilient might be 7. Be3, but then Black can still win material with 7...Bxe3 8. fxe3 Qh4+ 9. g3 Nxg3 10. hxg3 Qxh1 {{Chess/not|---}}. White resigns. == Theory table == {{ChessMid}} == References == {{reflist}} {{wikipedia|Petrov Defence}} {{Chess Opening Theory/Footer}}

{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Damiano variation |parent=[[../|Russian game]] |responses=[[/4. Qe2|4. Qe2]] }} == 3...Nxe4!? · Damiano variation == A sideline. Black takes back on e4 immediately, but despite appearances, Black doesn't get to keep material equality this way. With best play for Black this line is a pawn sacrifice for which Black obtains some compensation. [[/4. Qe2|'''4. Qe2''']] attacks the knight and sets up discoveries along the e-file that Black has opened. Black's best move is 4...Qe7, setting up a pin of their own after after 5. Qxe4. This leads to the Kholmov gambit: 5...d6 6. d4 dxe5 7. dxe5 Nc6{{Chess/not|+}} and Black wins the piece back at the cost of the d-pawn. '''4. Qf3?!''' may be played, hoping for Black to defend their knight 4...d5?? 5. Qxf2# instead of 4...Nf6 or 4...Ng5. '''4. d4''' may [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5/3...d6/4. Nf3/4...Nxe4/5. d4|transpose into a Classical attack]] after 4...d6 5. Nf3. === History === This line was introduced by [[w:Pedro Damiano|Pedro Damiano]] in his book, ''Libro da Imparare a Giocare a Scacchi'' (Italian: Book for learning to play chess), one of the oldest books on "modern rules" chess. Damiano gives 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nf6 3. Nxe5 Nxe4 4. Qe2 Qe7 (this is now known as the Kholmov gambit) 5. Qxe4 d6 6. d4 f6 7. f4 dxe5 8. dxe5 Nd7 9. Nc3 fxe5 10. Nd5 Qd6(??. 10...Nf6 is better) 11. fxe5 Qc6 12. Bb5 Qc5 13. Be3 to trap the queen.{{Cite book |title=The works of Damiano, Ruy-Lopez, and Salvio on the game of chess |last=Sarratt |first=J. pages.title: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4/3...exd4/4. Nxd4
pages.wikitext:
{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Scotch game |eco=[[Chess/ECOC|C45]] |parent=[[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4|Scotch game]] → [[../|3...exd4]] }} == 4. Nxd4 == Black has now an opportunity to take the initiative that should not be wasted. [[/4...Bc5|'''4...Bc5''']], the '''classical variation''', attacks White's central knight on d4 and forces White to either move it or protect it. Black should expect replies like 5. Be3, 5. Nxc6, or 5. Nb3. [[/4...Nf6|'''4...Nf6''']], the '''Schmidt variation''', is most common. Black puts immediate attacking pressure on White's pawn on e4. Rather than defend it with 5. Nc3 Bb4 (pinning the knight) 6. Nxc6 bxc6 7. Bd3, the main continuation is to trade off the knights and push it instead 5. Nxc6 bxc6 6. e5. [[/4...Qh4|'''4...Qh4''']], the '''Steinitz variation''', is more aggressive. Black threatens White's e-pawn and wins it outright after 5. Nc3 Bb4 6. Be2 (6. Bd2?? to unpin the knight drops the knight on d4) Qxe4. However, doing so costs time and White is thought to get more than enough compensation. The line continues 7. Nb5 Bxc3+ 8. bxc3 Kd8 9. O-O. [[/4...Qf6|'''4...Qf6''']] is a line where the Queen is developed to attack the knight. White can tranpose this to a classical Scotch with 5. c3; however it is more sharp to play 5. Nb5, threatening the now unprotected c7 fork. Black usually responds with 5... Bc5, threatening checkmate. After White defends, Black can play Bb6 protecting c7. White will then attempt to remove this bishop with their other knight. [[/4...Nxd4|'''4...Nxd4?''']] is a line more common at lower levels. This allows White to centralise their Queen early without potential tempo gains and is a mistake by Black. White usually wants to quickly castle queenside and counter a potential Nf6 with e5, similar to the ''Schmidt variation''. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}} '''1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4'''

pages.wikitext:
{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Scotch gambit |parent=[[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4|Scotch game]] → [[../|3...exd4]] }} == 4. Bc4 · Scotch gambit == White temporarily forgoes recapturing the d4 pawn, instead developing the light-squared bishop to the most active square targeting the f7 pawn. There's no great way for Black to hold on to the pawn they are temporarily up. [[/4...Bc5|'''4...Bc5''']], the '''Haxo gambit''' and second most common move, is the only way to add another defender to the pawn on d4. Though Black has two defenders to White's two attackers, after 5. c3 Black is best advised to give the pawn back. This is because 5...dxc3?, thinking White wants 6. Nxc3 and Black will still be ahead a pawn, loses to 6. Bxf7+! Kxf7 7. Qd5!+. White can recapture the bishop and if Black still tries to cling onto the material, they fall behind too far in position and development, e.g. 7...Ke8 8. Qh5+ (a little trick to either take the bishop with check or force Black to weaken their kingside) g6 9. Qxc5 cxb2 10. Bxb2{{chess/not|+++}}. Instead, Black's idea is to return the pawn with 5...Nf6, transposing into the Greco gambit for an even game, or 5...d3. [[/4...Nf6|'''4...Nf6''']] is the most played move, developing the knight and attacking the pawn on e4. This position can also arise out of the Italian game, after 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bc4 Nf6 4. d4 exd4. After 4...Nf6, White usually responds either with 5. e5, where they recover the pawn with the sequence 5. e5 d5 6. Bb5 Ne4 7. Nxd4 Bd7, or 5. O-O, sacrificing the ''other'' pawn by allowing 5...Nxe4, the '''double gambit accepted'''. 6. Re1 doesn't win the knight outright, rather the game continues 6...d5 7. Bxd5 Qxd5 8. Nc3! (d-pawn is pinned) and 9. Nxe4 after the queen moves. === Sidelines === [[/4...Bb4+|'''4...Bb4+''']], the '''London defence''', seeks to capitalise on Black's control of c3 while they can. 5. c3 dxc3 6. O-O cxb2 7. Bxb2 and while White is down two pawns, they have more than enough compensation in rapid development and activity. [[/4...Be7|'''4...Be7''']], is called the '''Benima defence'''. Black simply gets a piece off the back rank to make way for castling, and allows White to retake d4 straight away. This resembles the Hungarian defence to the Italian opening, if Black accepted the pawn on d4. Black's position is conservative: the bishop is not optimally placed on e7, but it is solid enough. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}} '''1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Bc4'''

=5. Nc3 · Caro-Kann Defence - Advance Variation, Van Der Wiel Attack=

A sounder response than [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. e5/3...Bf5/4. Nf3|4. Bd3]], and more ambitious than [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. e5/3...Bf5/4. Nf3|4. Nf3]], 4. Nc3 has helped revitalize the Advance Variation of the Caro-Kann.

White usually plans to harass Black's bishop with g4 and h4-h5, and Nc3 takes away the e4 square from the bishop.

It is almost always met with 4...e6, with black aiming ultimately to play c5.

== 4. h4 · Tal variation ==

White gains space on the king's side. 

Unlike in other variations of the advance Caro-Kann, Black cannot play '''4...e6?''' immediately, as 5. g4 would trap the bishop (5...Be4 6. f3 Bg6 7. h5). 

[[/4...h5|'''4...h5''']] is the main move, controlling g4 and so allowing Black to play ...e6 and ...Ne7. 

=== History ===

[[w:Mikhail Tal|Mikhail Tal]] played this line five times in his 1961 World Championship rematch against [[w:Mikhail Botvinnik|Mikhail Botvinnik]].<ref>[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1032562 Tal v Botvinnik, 1961 (round 10). Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4|Scotch game]] }} == 3...Nc6 == This is an uncommon way of playing the Philidor defence, as while the knight on c6 defends the e5 pawn, it may be pinned with Bb5. This position can arise in the Scotch game if Black declines to trade on d4 by playing 3...d6 instead. White attacks e5 twice and Black appears to defend it twice. If White trades in the centre, [[/4. dxe5|'''4. dxe5?!''']] Nxe5 5. Nxe5 dxe5 6. Qxd8+ Kxd8 Black loses castling rights, but the queens are off the board and the position is close to even. [[/4. Bb5|'''4. Bb5''']], pinning the knight to the king, removes a defender of e5 first. This is a transposition into the '''Old Steintiz defence''' in the Spanish game. The Stockfish choice is [[/4. d5|'''4. d5''']] Ne7 5. c4, closing the centre while gaining time on the knight and expanding on the queenside. Various other transpositions are possible: * '''4. Nc3''' transposes to the [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3|Three Knights Opening]]. * '''4. Bc4''' transposes to the [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...d6|Semi-Italian Opening]]. * '''4. c3''' transposes to the [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. c3|Ponziani Opening]]. ==Theory table== {{ChessTable}} {{ChessMid}} ==References== ===See also=== {{Wikipedia|Philidor Defence}} {{ChessFooter}}

== 3...Nd5 ==
This is obviously the only good move, as 3...Ne4?? 4.d3! forfeits the knight, whilst 3...Ng8? is way too passive and forfeits two tempi. White usually plays 4.d4 or 4.Nf3. If White played 4.Bc4, or 4.g3, Black is fine after e6 and eventually d6.<ref>https://www.chess.com/lessons/view/1145</ref>

== 3...Ng8? ==
This retreat is just too cowardly and timid. Black has lost two tempi moving the knight to g8 from f6. After d4, White has a huge center and initiative. 3...Nd5 is much better, since the knight is well placed there. It is usually unwise to move a piece back to it's original square in the opening.

== 3...Nf6 · Anti-Alapin gambit ==
"Death to the 2. c3 Sicilian!" proclaimed Lakdawala & Hansen, in their 2022 book on this line.<ref name="lakdawala">{{Cite book |title=The Anti-Alapin Gambit |last=Lakdawala |first=Cyrus |publisher=CarstenChess |year=2022 |isbn=978-87-93812-37-6 |location=Bayonne, New Jersey |last2=Hansen |first2=Carsten}}</ref> Black does not recapture the pawn immediately, but first develops their knight. This resembles the [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. f4/2...d5|Tal gambit after 2. f4!? d5 3. exd5 Nf6]]. 

=== Decline the gambit ===

'''4. d4''' offers back the pawn to Black. Black could retake 4...Qxd5, as in the Barman variation, 3...Qxd5, but this move order allows them to capture with the knight instead, 4...Nxd5. This avoids transposing into more familiar Alapin positions. White has fewer ways to gain tempo on the knight than the queen, and after 5. Nf3 cxd4 6. cxd4 the knight is already blockading the isolated pawn. Because after 4. d4 Nxd5 5. Nf3 cxd4, White also has the option of 6. Nxd4, the alternative move order 4...cxd4, aiming for 5. cxd4 Nxd5, is sometimes seen. 

=== Hold on to the pawn ===

By not retaking the pawn immediately, Black gives White the chance to defend it. In this sense it is a gambit: White can defend the d5 pawn with '''4. c4'''. Then, Black can play 4...e6 (threatens to take twice on d5 to recover the material) 5. exd6 Bxd6. Though White is up a pawn in material, Black has sufficient compensation in the form of activity. Black has two pieces developed and is ready to develop their king's bishop, while White has nothing developed. The game is about even. (White can't really avoid exd6 in this line. If 5. Qe2? to pin the pawn, then after ...Bd6 and ...O-O White is left with the same choice, and now their queen is mis-placed too). 

'''4. Bb5+''' first is a slight improvement. This seems more natural because it gets the bishop to an active square before blocking it with c4, and gets White closer to castling. If Black should trade off their light-square bishop (4...Bd7 5. Bxd7+ Qxd7), then without the bishop to recapture, Black's ...e6 idea is less potent: 6. c4 e6 7. Qe2! Bd6 8. dxe6 Qxe6 9. Qxe6+ fxe6 {{chess/not|+}}. Blocking the check with the knight is more common: 4...Nbd7 5. c4 a6 6. Bxd7 Bxd7 (6...Qxd7 is the recommendation of Lakdawala & Hansen)<ref name="lakdawala" /> and Black still has this idea of ...e6 dxe6 Bxe6. 7. d4! is a useful inclusion, where 7...e6 8. dxe6 Bxe6 9. d5! Bf5 {{chess/not|+}}, or 7...cxd4 8. Qxd4. Black does not have ...Nc6 to chase the queen, and this adds a defender to d5, so 8...e6 and White doesn't even have to take the pawn. 

'''4. Qa5+!''' is a way of hanging on to the pawn without losing the bishop pair. After 4...Nbd7 5. c4, if Black plays 5...e6 they must recapture with their f-pawn instead of their bishop. (The engine idea is the startling pawn sacrifice 5...b5! 6. Qxb5 Rb8 7. Qa4. Black can then play 7...Rb6 8. Nf3 e6 and recapture with the rook, 9. dxe6 Rxe6+). If 4...Bd7 instead, 5. Qb3 (attacks the b7 pawn) Qb6. If White tries to secure the pawn with 6. c4 now, the c-pawn hangs at the end of 6...e6 7. Qxb6 (to prevent ...Qxe6) axb6 8. dxe6 Bxe6 {{chess/not|=}} and Black has equalised. 6. Bc4! is a better way to defend the pawn. 6...e6? 7. dxe6 Bxe6 8. Bxe6 Qxe6+ 9. Qxe6+ fxe6 {{chess/not|++}}, White is up a pawn in the endgame. Black can try for 6...Na6 followed by ...Nc7 to win back the pawn instead.

=== History ===

3...Nf6 was recorded in the British Championship in 1959, however the game continued 4. d4 Qxd5, transposing into the Barman variation.<ref>[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1161368 Milner-Barry v Littlewood, 1959. Chessgames.com]</ref> 

Lakdawala & Hansen attribute some of the popularity of the line to it having been played by Magnus Carlsen in the Chessable Masters tournament in 2022.<ref name="lakdawala" /><ref>[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=2280396 Grandelius v Carlsen, 2022. Chessgames.com]</ref>

A recent high-level appearance was at the 2023 World Blitz Championship, in a game between Ian Nepomniachtchi and Arjun Erigaisi.<ref>[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=2635583 Nepomniachtchi v Erigaisi, 2023. Chessgames.com]</ref>

* [[/5. d4|5. d4 · Classical attack]] * [[/5. Nc3|5. Nc3 · Nimzowitsch attack]] * [[/5. Qe2|5. Qe2 · Cozio attack]] }} == 4. Nxe4 == Black captures the pawn and material is now equal. White would like to take some control of the centre, develop, and ideally force Black to move or lose their advanced knight. They have several options. === Take the centre === [[/5. d4|'''5. d4''']], the '''Classical attack''', is the most principled move and the mainline. White prioritises taking space in the centre. Next they may develop their bishop behind their pawn. After 5...d5 6. Bd3 White is ready to castle, but Black's knight is dug in on e4. White will try to increase pressure on the knight with moves like c4 and Nc3, hoping to win some concession. === Develop pieces === [[/5. Nc3|'''5. Nc3''']], the '''Nimzowitsch attack''', is the chief sideline. White offers a trade of knights, and after 5...Nxc3 6. dxc3, Black's knight is gone and White has doubled pawns in exchange for rapid development. === Attack the knight === Alternatively White can prioritise kicking the knight first. [[/5. Qe2|'''5. Qe2''']], the '''Cozio attack''', is the most common continuation at the amateur level. White pins Black's knight to the queen. Defending it with 5...d5? fails to 6. d3. Black's only move to unpin and defend the knight is 5...Qe7. After 6. d3 Nf6, the position leads to an exchange of queens and an early endgame. [[/5. d3|'''5. d3''']], the '''French attack''', kicks the knight away immediately with a pawn. After 5...Nf6, the main moves are 6. d4, important for opening up White's bishop, and 6...d5, transposing into an [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. d4/2...d5/3. exd5/3...exd5/4. Nf3/4...Nf6|Exchange French]]. [[/5. Bd3|'''5. Bd3''']], the '''Millennium attack''' is a rarely played sideline. Compared to 5. d4 and 6. Bd3, Black isn't in time to play 5...d5 to defend the knight, so has to move it away instead. However, as White's bishop now obstructs their d-pawn they will soon have to move it again (usually to c3: 5...Nf6 6. O-O Be7 7. c3 O-O 8. Bc2 Bg4 9. d4). [[/5. c4|'''5. c4''']], the '''Kaufman attack''', the idea being to prevent Black from advancing his pawn to d5 so that so that after d4 and Bd3, Black's knight is still loose and they must move it. =Theory table= {{ChessTable}} '''1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nf6 3. Nxe5 d6 4. Nf3 Nxe4'''

= Scotch Game, Classical Variation =
White continues with 5. Nxc6. Black has a few options here: 5...dxc6, 5...bxc6, and 5...Qf6.

The first option, 5...dxc6?! loses castling rights to 6. Qxd8+ Kxd8, though.

The second option, 5...bxc6, is more common and continues in natural Classical development with the Bishop going to d3 and c4, the Knight usually to c3 and kingside castling.

The final option, 5...Qf6, is most common. Black attacks f2, threatening checkmate, and the knight on c6. White has no way to defend both at once, and must give back the knight. 6. Qd2 and 6. Qf3 are the most popular defenses to the Intermezzo.

== 4.d4 ==
This move gains central space and connects with the e-pawn. White has created a pawn chain in the center and is now threatening c4 followed by d5, when Black would really suffocate by his lack of central space. This pawn controls White's center.

== 5. Nc3 · Nimzowitsch attack ==
This move is played if White wants to imbalance the position in the otherwise dull and symmetrical Petrov. 

White offers a knight trade. Taking it, [[/5...Nxc3|'''5...Nxc3''']], is the main move, and after 6. dxc3 White has open lines but doubled pawns. 

'''5...Nf6''' is an alternative.

[[w:Viswanathan Anand|Viswanathan Anand]] once played '''5...Bf5??''' in this position, and resigned after 6. Qe2: the knight is pinned and there is no saving it.<ref>[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1018015 Zapata v Anand, 1988. Chessgames.com]</ref>

= Petrov's Defense =
{{Chess Opening Theory/Position|Petrov's Defense||rd|nd|bd|qd|kd|bd||rd|pd|pd|pd|||pd|pd|pd||||pd||||||||||||||||pl|nd|||||||||nl|||pl|pl|pl|||pl|pl|pl|rl|nl|bl|ql|kl|bl||rl||}}The Classical Attack in the Petrov is the most popular continuation to Black's natural 4...Nxe4. The overwhelmingly popular 5...d5 defends the knight and defends the center; White will attempt to attack Black's e4 knight and attack Black's d5 pawn with Bd3 and c4 respectively while Black will defend against White's ideas with all their might.


As mentioned above, 5...d5 is almost 20 times more popular than the second most popular move, 5...Be7, which often transposes into the main lines of the Classical Attack. Most Petrov lines have a higher than average draw percentage due to the highly symmetrical positions in the opening.{{wikipedia|Petrov's Defence}}

Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6.Bg5 Nbd7''' This knight move is a natural one in the Najdorf, and it also stops Bxf6, doubling the Black pawns. Although not as popular as the move 6...e6, it is a solid, respectable alternative to the main line. Both sides will usually castle queenside. Black, using his knights and light-squared bishop, will attempt to pressure e4. White, on the other hand, will try to get play on the a2-g8 diagonal and the central files. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}}. '''1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.
